title: 第二盘脆得直响  (Batch Two Crunches Loudly)

segments.t: Five minutes later, Peng proudly sets Tin Two on the wooden cooling board while his younger brother Hao steps into the café corner sniffing the sweet caramel air beside Mei. Let us listen in first.
快过来，好弟弟！闻闻二号盘上这层烤香的黄糖脆壳！
闻起来真像热闹的老街集市，哥哥，不过上面亮得有点吓人。
志鹏，刚才在热烤箱里，你到底撒了多少勺粗糖呀？
够让叉子按下去的时候，每一块都发出清脆的响声！
让我把小叉子轻轻往正中间按下去……敲、敲、当！
哎呀——志鹏，蛋糕可不该敲出前台门铃的声音呀！
从建筑师的专业角度来看，我们能用第二盘给车棚铺屋顶了。
嘿！敲开上面那扇糖窗户，尝尝底下温热的杏仁蛋糕嘛！
嗯，在这顶硬糖头盔底下，莓果和碎杏仁真好吃！
看来单用柠檬太酸，单用干糖又烤成院子石板了。
小美，那块蓝水痕底下，到底藏着什么又软又亮的糖霜呢？
快把那本绿草本书再拿来——我们的鼻子说不定比眼睛还灵！
Now let's go through it line by line with the English translation.
快过来，好弟弟！闻闻二号盘上这层烤香的黄糖脆壳！

'Step right up, little brother! Smell this toasted brown-sugar crisp crust on Tin Two!' Doubling "wen" ("smell") into "wenwen" invites a quick sniff, while "ceng" counts flat layers like a crust or coat of glaze.
闻起来真像热闹的老街集市，哥哥，不过上面亮得有点吓人。

'It smells just like a lively old-street market, big brother, though the top shines a bit alarmingly.' Adding "qilai" to "wen" builds "wen qilai" ("smells like..."), Mandarin's everyday way to report a first sensory impression.
志鹏，刚才在热烤箱里，你到底撒了多少勺粗糖呀？

'Peng, just how many spoons of coarse sugar did you sprinkle inside that hot oven?' Slipping "daodi" ahead of a question literally adds pressing curiosity—"on earth / actually how many spoons did you use?"
够让叉子按下去的时候，每一块都发出清脆的响声！
'Enough so that when your fork presses down, every single slice gives a crisp snap!' "Qingcui" combines "clear" and "crisp" for a clean crunching sound, paired with "an xiaqu" ("press downward").
让我把小叉子轻轻往正中间按下去……敲、敲、当！
'Let me press my small fork gently right in the middle... tap, tap, clang!' "Wang zheng zhongjian" aims "straight toward the exact centre", right before metallic "dang!" rings out on the hard sugar.
哎呀——志鹏，蛋糕可不该敲出前台门铃的声音呀！
'Oh dear—a cake is definitely not supposed to ring like the front-desk bell, Peng!' Warm "aiya" lets out dismayed surprise, and "bu gai" literally means "should not" or "is not supposed to".
从建筑师的专业角度来看，我们能用第二盘给车棚铺屋顶了。

'Looking from an architect's professional angle, we could roof the bike shed with Batch Two.' "Jianzhushi" literally adds specialist "shi" ("master") to "jianzhu" ("architecture"), while "pu wuding" literally means laying a roof.
嘿！敲开上面那扇糖窗户，尝尝底下温热的杏仁蛋糕嘛！

'Hey! Break open that sugar window on top and taste the warm almond cake underneath!' Peng leans into the joke with "shan"—the counter for doors and windows—for his glassy "tang chuanghu" ("sugar window").
嗯，在这顶硬糖头盔底下，莓果和碎杏仁真好吃！

'Mmm, underneath this hard sugar helmet, the berries and crushed almonds are delicious!' Hats and helmets take the counter "ding" ("crown/top"), framing Hao's joke about a "ying tang toukui" ("hard sugar helmet").
看来单用柠檬太酸，单用干糖又烤成院子石板了。

'So lemon alone is too sour, and dry sugar alone bakes into courtyard flagstone.' Repeating "dan yong" ("using alone") contrasts the two extremes neatly, ending on "shiban" ("stone slab / flagstone").
小美，那块蓝水痕底下，到底藏着什么又软又亮的糖霜呢？
'What soft, shiny glaze could possibly be hiding underneath that blue stain, Mei?' Using "you... you..." in "you ruan you liang" stacks two qualities side by side: "both soft and shiny".
快把那本绿草本书再拿来——我们的鼻子说不定比眼睛还灵！

'Bring me that green herb book again—our noses might work even sharper than our eyes!' "Shuobuding" ("cannot say for sure") is natural spoken Mandarin for "maybe/might", and "ling" literally means quick and keen.
Now let's listen to the whole conversation one last time.
快过来，好弟弟！闻闻二号盘上这层烤香的黄糖脆壳！

让我把小叉子轻轻往正中间按下去……敲、敲、当！
哎呀——志鹏，蛋糕可不该敲出前台门铃的声音呀！

嗯，在这顶硬糖头盔底下，莓果和碎杏仁真好吃！
看来单用柠檬太酸，单用干糖又烤成院子石板了。
小美，那块蓝水痕底下，到底藏着什么又软又亮的糖霜呢？
快把那本绿草本书再拿来——我们的鼻子说不定比眼睛还灵！
Batch Two could survive a hailstorm on a shed roof, sending Mei back to the old botanical book for one more clue! See you next time.
回头见！
